title: Food Delivery System
summary: Customers order from restaurants, a delivery partner is assigned, and the order moves through a state machine to delivery.
problem: Design the object model of a food delivery service. A customer browses a restaurant menu, places an order, and pays. The restaurant accepts and prepares it, a delivery partner is assigned to pick it up, and the customer receives it. The total depends on item prices, a delivery fee and optional discounts.
functional: Restaurants have menus of items with a price and an availability flag
A customer places an order with one or more items from a single restaurant; the order records the price of each item at the time of ordering
An order moves through well-defined states (placed, accepted, preparing, ready, picked up, delivered) and can be cancelled or rejected only from states where that makes sense
When an order is ready (or accepted, if you pre-assign), the system assigns an available delivery partner using a replaceable strategy such as nearest partner
The order total is computed from item prices, a delivery fee and zero or more discounts (percentage off, flat off, free delivery above an amount)
Interested parties (customer, restaurant, partner) are told when an order changes state
nonFunctional: Adding a new discount type or a new assignment strategy must not change existing classes
An illegal transition (for example delivered to preparing) is rejected, not silently applied
Two orders must never be assigned the same delivery partner at the same time, even when assignments run concurrently
A later change to a menu price must not change the total of an order already placed
constraints: In-memory design is enough; persistence, maps and real payment gateways are out of scope
A partner carries at most one order at a time (batching several orders is an extension)
Locations can be reduced to a simple (latitude, longitude) pair and a distance function
deliverables: A class diagram (Mermaid or an uploaded image) with the relationships between classes
The order state machine as a diagram or a transition table, including who triggers each transition
The responsibility of each class in a sentence
The design patterns you used and where, or why you used none
How you prevent double assignment of a partner
Optional: code for the order state machine and one discount rule
hints: Treat the price of an item at order time as a copy stored on the order line, not a reference to the live menu item.
Pricing is a pipeline of rules applied to a running total; each rule is one small class behind one interface.
The order state machine can be an enum with a table of allowed transitions, or one class per state. Both work; decide which suits the number of states and the behaviour attached to each.
Assigning a partner is a claim: the check that the partner is free and the change to busy must happen as one atomic step.
reference:
This is one reasonable design, not the only valid one. The alternatives are named where they matter.

### Classes
- `Restaurant` owns a `Menu`, a list of `MenuItem` (id, name, price as `Money`, available).
- `Customer` and `DeliveryPartner` (id, location, status: AVAILABLE, ASSIGNED, OFFLINE).
- `Order` is the aggregate: customer, restaurant, a list of `OrderLine` (item name, unit price copied at order time, quantity), a status, an optional partner, and a price breakdown. It enforces its own state transitions.
- `OrderService` is the facade used by the API: `place`, `accept`, `markReady`, `cancel`, `deliver`.
- `PricingEngine` applies an ordered list of `PricingRule` objects (strategy). Rules: `DeliveryFeeRule`, `PercentageDiscount`, `FlatDiscount`, `FreeDeliveryAbove`.
- `PartnerAssigner` (strategy interface) with `NearestPartnerAssigner`; a `PartnerPool` holds the partners and does the atomic claim.
- `OrderEventListener` (observer) with `NotificationListener`; `OrderService` publishes an event on every transition.

### Order state machine
PLACED -> ACCEPTED (restaurant) -> PREPARING (restaurant) -> READY (restaurant) -> PICKED_UP (partner) -> DELIVERED (partner).
PLACED -> REJECTED (restaurant, or timeout). PLACED, ACCEPTED -> CANCELLED (customer); PREPARING -> CANCELLED only by the restaurant or support, with a cancellation fee. After PICKED_UP there is no cancellation, only a refund process outside this model.

`Order.transitionTo` looks the move up in a table `Map<OrderStatus, Set<OrderStatus>>` and throws on an illegal one. That keeps every rule in one place and gives the unit test a single table to cover.

### Pricing as a strategy pipeline
`PricingEngine` starts from the sum of `unitPrice * quantity` and passes the running amount through each rule in a defined order (discounts first, then fees, then tax, for example). Order matters: a 10% discount before the delivery fee is not the same as after it, so the order is part of the contract and is tested. The breakdown (subtotal, discounts, fee, total) is stored on the order so it can be shown and audited without recomputing. Money is an integer number of minor units, never a float.

### Assignment and concurrency
`NearestPartnerAssigner` ranks available partners by distance and tries to `tryClaim` the best one. `tryClaim` is an atomic compare-and-set from AVAILABLE to ASSIGNED (a lock per partner, a CAS on the status, or a conditional UPDATE in a database). If the claim fails because another order got there first, it tries the next candidate. If nobody is free the order stays READY and is retried by a timer. If the partner declines or times out, the partner is released and the assigner runs again with that partner excluded.

### Trade-offs and alternatives
- **State machine: table vs State pattern.** A transition table is the smallest thing that works and is easy to test. One class per state is worthwhile when each state has significant different behaviour (for example, different cancellation fees and side effects). With about eight states and little per-state behaviour, the table is usually enough; the State pattern is the reasonable choice if behaviour grows.
- **Price snapshot vs live reference.** Copying the price onto the order line costs a little duplication but protects history. The alternative, versioned menu items, is heavier and only pays off if you also need menu history for other reasons.
- **Discounts: strategy list vs decorator vs chain of responsibility.** A list of rules is simplest. Decorators suit stacking where each wraps the next; a chain suits rules that can stop the pipeline (for example an exclusive coupon). Pick based on whether rules interact.
- **Assign at accept time or at ready time.** Assigning early cuts waiting but may leave the partner idle at the restaurant; assigning late reduces idle time but may delay pickup. Real systems often assign when the estimated preparation time is close to the travel time.
- **Push to one partner vs offer to several.** Offering to one partner at a time is simple and avoids conflicts; broadcasting to a few and taking the first accept is faster but needs the atomic claim above.
- **Events: synchronous observers vs a message queue.** In-process listeners are fine for this exercise; in production notifications go through a queue so a slow SMS provider cannot slow down a state change.
- **Out of scope but worth naming:** batching several orders per partner, surge pricing, refunds, restaurant opening hours, and persisting the order with optimistic locking (a version column) so two concurrent transitions cannot both succeed.
